title: Beautiful Array
statement:
Arrange the integers `1` to `n` into an array `nums`, using each exactly once, so that no element is the average of two elements on either side of it. In other words, for every choice of indices `i < k < j`, `2 * nums[k]` must not equal `nums[i] + nums[j]`.

Return any arrangement with this property. One always exists for every allowed `n`, and every valid arrangement is accepted.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying permutations until one passes is exponential, so the answer has to be built. Two facts make that easy:

- If an array is beautiful, mapping every value through `x -> 2x - 1` or `x -> 2x` keeps it beautiful, because the rule `2 * nums[k] = nums[i] + nums[j]` is linear and survives scaling and shifting.
- If every odd number comes before every even number, a pair with one odd and one even end has an odd sum, so no whole number can be its average.

So solve a half-size problem, turn one copy into the odd numbers and another into the even numbers, and put the odd part first.

## Approach

1. `build(1)` is `[1]`.
2. For a larger `size`, there are `ceil(size / 2)` odd numbers and `floor(size / 2)` even numbers in `1..size`.
3. Build those two smaller arrays recursively; map the first with `2x - 1` into `odds` and the second with `2x` into `evens`.
4. Join `odds` then `evens` into `result`, store it in `memo` and return it.

## Example 1, step by step

For `n = 4`, `build(4)` calls `build(2)`, which calls `build(1) = [1]` twice and returns `[1] + [2] = [1, 2]`. Back in `build(4)`, `odds = [1, 3]` and `evens` reuses `[1, 2]` from `memo` to give `[2, 4]`, so the answer is `[1, 3, 2, 4]`. LeetCode shows `[2, 1, 4, 3]`; both are beautiful, and any valid answer is accepted.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each level of halving has at most two distinct sizes, each built once, so the work is about n + n/2 + n/4 + ... per size.
- Space: O(n) for the stored arrays, plus O(log n) recursion depth.

## Pitfalls

- The odd half must have `ceil(size / 2)` values and the even half `floor(size / 2)`; swapping them produces numbers above `n` or misses some.
- Keep the two halves apart: interleaving odd and even values brings back pairs with an even sum and a possible average between them.
- Checking a candidate needs all pairs, not only neighbours: the average may sit anywhere between the two ends.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `memo` | finished arrays by size, so repeated sizes are built once |
| `size` | length of the beautiful array being built |
| `odds` | the half-size answer mapped to odd values with `2x - 1` |
| `evens` | the half-size answer mapped to even values with `2x` |
| `result` | `odds` followed by `evens`, a beautiful array of length `size` |

narration.2: Remember finished arrays by length; the same sizes come up again and again.
narration.4: build(size) returns a beautiful arrangement of 1..size.
narration.5: A single number is beautiful on its own.
narration.8: Has this size been built before?
narration.11: Solve the smaller problem for the ceil(size/2) odd values and map each x to 2x - 1.
narration.12: Solve it for the floor(size/2) even values and map each x to 2x.
narration.13: Odds first, evens second: a pair across the halves has an odd sum, so it has no whole-number average.
narration.14: Store the array for later calls of the same size.
narration.15: Hand the arrangement back to the caller.
